registryLegalName: Sealing of Records After Decriminalization of an Offence (NRS 179.271)

primaryStatutoryAuthority.description: Sealing of records after decriminalization of offense. The section provides a route where the conduct underlying a Nevada record is no longer a crime. The controlling review records the instrument as a written request rather than a full petition and classifies the track on that basis.

verificationStatute.description: No verification or notarization statute is identified for NRS 179.271, and the instrument itself is unread. Nothing is filled.

presentation.verificationPenaltyLabel: the penalties for a false statement

counselFlags: Record sealing, never expungement. The Nevada Department of Public Safety states directly that sealing is not expungement because it does not authorise destruction of the records.
Sealing does not restore firearm rights. Only a pardon that does not restrict the right to bear arms does.
Nevada orders do not bind out-of-state agencies and do not reach federal, tribal, military or out-of-state records.

Waiting period: not established by the review beyond the decriminalisation itself. Whether any waiting period applies under NRS 179.271 is part of the unread statutory text and must not be stated to a participant.

Filing vehicle unsettled: the controlling review describes the NRS 179.271 instrument as a written request rather than a full petition, but did not reproduce the section. Until the text is read, neither a request nor a petition may be drafted.
No verification or notarization statute is identified for NRS 179.271, and the instrument itself is unread. Nothing is filled.
Scope: any offence that remains a crime in Nevada is excluded, as are records held outside Nevada, which a Nevada order does not reach.

Under NRS 179.285 the proceedings are deemed never to have occurred and civil rights are restored, but NRS 179.295 allows sealed records to be reopened and NRS 179.301 allows certain persons and agencies to inspect them.
